3.4 Relative Velocity: Activity 3.1 ● You are following a child running at 20 ms-1 while you are running at 50 ms-1 . Initially, the child is 300 meters ahead of you. Estimate the time it will take for you to catch up with the child.

Certainly, here the child covers 20m in a second and the man following it covers 50m in the same one second i.e., a total of 50 -20 =30 m closer in 1 second. Hence every second elapse, the man gets by 30 m closer to the child. In doing so 300m distance will be covered in 300 = 10 second.
Hence you meet the child after 10 seconds.

To solve the problem mathematically, one must have the knowledge of relative velocity as 50-20 =30ms-1. The value 50- 20 = 30ms-1. Hence is the relative velocity of your with respect to the child. The 20ms-1 in your velocity as 50ms-1 = 30ms-1 + 20ms-1 and the child’s velocity 20ms-1 remains vain and the child completely comes at rest on subtracting 20ms-1 from your 50 ms-1. Hence the time taken to meet the child, t = v = 300 = 10 s. t 30 Examples: ● If you run in rainy weather, the rain appears as if it is coming towards you. ● If two vehicles pass each other along a straight road, the passengers in one vehicle perceive the other vehicle as moving with double the speed compared to what is observed by a stationary observer. ● If we observe a flying airplane from a moving bus, we perceive its motion differently compared to what is observed from the stationary ground. The disparity in perception, as studied so far, is known as relative motion. ● To determine the relative motion of a body with respect to a second body, the second body must be brought to rest. Therefore, the motion of one body with respect to another is considered as fixed to compare their relative velocities.

Some basic rules to find relative velocity: ● Let two bodies A and B be moving with velocities VA and VB in a direction. Then the velocity of A with respect to B is VAB = VA – VB, and the velocity of B with respect to A is VBA = VB - VA. ● If the bodies are moving in opposite directions, then the relative velocity of A with respect to B, VAB, is calculated as VA - (-VB), and the relative velocity of B with respect to A, VBA, is calculated as VB - (-VA). In case of two bodies moving in the opposite directions, the relative velocity gets added and that results a greater value than its absolute value. ● For two bodies acting at an acute angle (0 < θ < 90˚), to determine the relative velocity of an object with respect to an observer, the velocity of the observer is reversed, and a parallelogram is constructed. The diagonal of this parallelogram represents the relative velocity. The same technique can also be applied using the triangle law of velocity. Example:

Swimming Case:

i) For a person swimming in water, let Vpw be the velocity of the swimmer with respect to the water, and Vwg be the velocity of the water with respect to the ground. Then, Vpg = Vpw + Vwg, which implies Vpw = Vpg - Vwg.
Therefore, when swimming in the direction of the flow of water, Vpg = Vpw + Vwg, and when swimming in the opposite direction to the flow of water, Vpg = Vpw - Vwg.
Falling Rain Case:

● For vertical rain, it appears to fall vertically to an observer at rest. We say the relative velocity of the rain with respect to the observer is in the vertical direction. However, to an observer in motion, the situation is different. Let Vr be the velocity of the rain falling vertically, and Vp be the velocity of the person moving horizontally.
